title: By grace, not of yourselves (Ephesians 2:8–10)
hookLine: saved by grace through faith, created for good works

cards: On October thirty-first, 1999, in the German city of Augsburg, representatives of the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration.
It was about a question that had divided them since the sixteenth century: how is a person made right with God? Today's verses sat near the center of that long argument.
They come from Ephesians, the first of a new stretch of letters. Tradition says Paul wrote them as a prisoner, in chains.

teach.b: Ephesians chapter two starts with a hard picture: you were dead in your sins. Then the turn: God, who is rich in mercy, brought us to life with Christ.
Then the verses: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God; Not of works, that no man may glory." A gift. Not wages.
Nobody can take credit for it.

But Paul doesn't stop there, and readers who stop at verse nine miss the next line: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them."
Saved by grace, and made for good works. Not saved by good works, and not saved from doing them. The works were prepared in advance, like a path laid down for you to walk on.
The Greek word for workmanship is poiēma: something made, a crafted thing. Here it means God's handiwork. Catholics and Protestants argued for centuries over how grace, faith and works fit together.
The Catholic Church taught at the Council of Trent that nothing before justification, neither faith nor works, earns the grace of justification.

And in the 1999 declaration, Catholics and Lutherans said together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ, and not because of any merit, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts and calls us to good works.

teach.h: BY GRACE YOU ARE SAVED THROUGH FAITH.
teach.b: Some differences remain, and both sides say so. But on this, they found they could speak with one voice.

how: Catholics teach that justification is a free gift of grace that no one can merit, and that grace also makes good works possible; in 1999 the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration on justification.

o: a reward for those who keep every commandment
the short prayer of thanks said before a meal
saved as a gift from God, not as wages earned

games.q: inside the verses — tap the pairs.

s: Ephesians 2 says good works don't matter
verse ten: we are created in Christ Jesus in good works.
Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification
the Council of Trent taught that works earn the first grace of justification
Trent said nothing before justification, faith or works, merits it.

games.q: you've been saved by grace, a gift you didn't earn. according to Ephesians, what comes next?
o: pay it back by earning it with good works.
walk in the good works God prepared for you.
games.why: "we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus in good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them."

practice: Turn your hands palm up on your knees and think of one good thing you didn't earn: a person, your health, a morning, your faith if you have it.

Then turn your hands over, ready to work, and think of one good thing that seems to be waiting for you to do. If you pray, give thanks, then ask for help to do it; if not, simply receive, then decide.

wordCard.voice: By grace. Paul's words to the Ephesians: saved by God's gift, not by works, and then made for the good works God prepared. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: something made, a work (Ephesians 2:10); here, God's handiwork.

carryVoice: Your line: his workmanship. A gift first, then a path to walk. See you tomorrow.
